articles.title: In 1984, Johnny Carson bought a 4-acre Malibu estate for about $9.5 million; decades later, subsequent owners asked $81.5 million before the property finally sold for $40 million after major price cuts
articles.summary: US News: Johnny Carson’s former Malibu estate has had a remarkable journey through the luxury property market, moving from a roughly $9.5 million purchase in t.
articles.body: Johnny Carson’s former Malibu estate has had a remarkable journey through the luxury property market, moving from a roughly $9.5 million purchase in the 1980s to an $81.5 million asking price decades later before eventually changing hands for $40 million. The figures and property history were reported by the Mansion Global, with property records cited in their coverage. The late “Tonight Show” host bought the Point Dume estate in 1984 for about $9.5 million, according to the Los Angeles Times. Carson owned the property for more than two decades and continued to live there until his death in 2005 at the age of 79. The Malibu property was built in 1978 by architect Ed Niles and sits on slightly more than four acres overlooking the Pacific.At the heart of the compound is a 7,083-square-foot modern home featuring a copper-and-glass sunken fireplace, media room, wine cellar and an indoor arboretum beneath a 30-foot-high glass ceiling. The estate also includes extensive outdoor spaces, a swimming pool, waterfalls, a koi pond and a sunken tennis court.From Carson’s home to an $81.5 million listingAfter Carson’s death, the property passed to his widow, Alexis. In 2007, she sold the home and its adjacent parcels to fashion mogul and film producer Sidney Kimmel and his wife, Caroline. The Los Angeles Times reported the transaction at about $46 million, while later coverage cited property records putting the figure at $36.5 million, reflecting differences in how the multi-parcel deal was reported.A decade later, the Kimmels put the compound on the market for a staggering $81.5 million. The listing price was nearly nine times what Carson had paid for the estate in 1984. The property offered considerably more than just the main residence. A separate guesthouse stood on the adjoining land, while the tennis area included a pavilion with additional facilities. Its oceanfront setting and connection to one of American television’s most recognizable hosts added to its celebrity appeal. But the $81.5 million asking price did not translate into a sale.Price cut still could not secure a buyerBy August 2018, the asking price had been reduced to $65.2 million, an approximately 20% cut from the original listing price, the Los Angeles Times reported. Even at that lower figure, the estate remained on the market. The eventual sale came in June 2019, when the compound changed hands for $40 million. Mansion Global reported that the main house accounted for $25.9 million, while the two adjacent lots together sold for $14.1 million. That represented roughly a 51% reduction from the original $81.5 million asking price.The deal was still above the price cited by Mansion Global for the Kimmels’ 2007 acquisition, but it was far below the ambitious figure attached to the property when it first returned to the market in 2017. The buyer’s identity was not publicly established in the 2019 report, with Mansion Global noting that the property was acquired through a limited liability company. Later reporting identified venture capitalist Riaz Valani and his wife, Augusta Tigrett, as the buyers in an off-market transaction valued at $40 million.The estate’s price history ultimately tells a striking story of Malibu luxury real estate: Carson’s roughly $9.5 million purchase in 1984 became a $46 million-or-thereabouts transaction in 2007, an $81.5 million asking price in 2017 and, after a major reduction, a $40 million sale in 2019. The property has since returned to the market, with a $110 million asking price reported in 2025.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: In 2024, Alabama turned three Fish River sites red, using harmless dye in a time-of-journey study to help build model pollution in the Weeks Bay watershed
articles.summary: US News: In a unique effort to protect the ecological health of Weeks Bay, Alabama introduced harmless Rhodamine dye into the Fish River to study water flow and pollution dispersion. This innovative four-day research initiative aims to enhance water quality management for the area's vital wildlife and shellfish populations.
articles.body: Weeks Bay quietly performs a lot of work along Alabama's Gulf Coast that most tourists are unaware of. This little estuary near Fairhope, fed by the Fish River and the Magnolia River, filters waters before it reaches Mobile Bay, providing nursery grounds for prawns, oysters and the young of numerous fish species that eventually appear on dinner plates around the area. Understanding precisely how water and whatever it contains flows through that system is essential to maintaining its health, but the issue is a far more difficult subject than it may seem.The Alabama Department of Environmental Management sought to answer that question with four days of research in the summer of 2024. The agency said it injected a bright red substance called Rhodamine dye at three sites along the river over four days, between July 29 and August 1, in addition to collecting streamflow and water quality data.Why the river ran crimsonDespite its bright colour, ADEM said the dye is used in small amounts for time-of-travel studies. The agency discharged the dye at three crossings on the Fish River at US Highway 90, Alabama Highway 104 and Baldwin County Road 32, then measured how long it took the colour to travel downstream towards Weeks Bay. The dye is visible to the human eye, can be sampled in small quantities, and allows scientists to assess how swiftly water truly flows through a river system, not estimates based on the shape of the channel alone.That is a more important distinction than it sounds. Pollutants upstream don't always move at a predictable pace, and the top of a river can be calm while the water below is moving at widely varying speeds, depending on rainfall, tides, and the shape of the riverbed. In addition to tracking the dye, ADEM workers also tested discharges from wastewater treatment facilities that empty into the watershed to provide a clearer picture of what goes into the system and how fast it is moving through.Making colour into a working modelThe larger goal behind the exercise was to gather the raw material needed to build and calibrate a water quality model of the entire Weeks Bay watershed, a computer-based tool that can simulate how pollutants spread through the Fish River, the Magnolia River and the bay itself under different conditions. Once the model is built, instead of responding solely when water quality concerns arise, authorities may be able to anticipate the likely impact of a planned construction, a new discharge permit or a spell of heavy rain.Watersheds of this type border a national system of protected estuaries. Weeks Bay is a National Estuarine Research Reserve of NOAA, a classification it has had since 1986 because its mix of tidal marsh, wooded wetland and pitcher plant bog represents a broader slice of the Mobile Bay ecosystem worth preservation for long-term study. Reserve staff currently collect water quality data from sites across the bay, and a well-calibrated model based on ADEM’s fieldwork might further improve those long-running records.A splash of colour for a lasting impressionA few days of fieldwork, a couple of Rhodamine injections and careful sampling yielded data that could influence how the Weeks Bay watershed is managed for years to come. Residents near the Fish River saw the dye study unfold in real time. For an estuary that supports shellfish and fish nurseries along the Gulf Coast, the temporary dye study could provide a clearer picture of how pollution travels through the water.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: An American citizen was arrested at Atlanta airport for wiping his phone with PIN during airport search; here's what new Court ruling says on phone and laptop searches
articles.summary: Tech News News: An American citizen was arrested at Atlanta airport after his phone was wiped when he entered a PIN during an airport search in January this year. Mon.
articles.body: An American citizen was arrested at Atlanta airport after his phone was wiped when he entered a PIN during an airport search in January this year. Months later, a new US court ruling has highlighted just how much power border authorities have when it comes to searching travellers’ electronic devices. The January case of Atlanta resident Samuel Tunick involved GrapheneOS, a privacy-focused Android operating system that has a feature allowing users to wipe a phone with a designated PIN. Prosecutors accused Tunick of destroying potential evidence. His lawyers have challenged the search and the seizure of his phone.Now, the US Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit has ruled in a separate case that border agents can search a traveller’s cellphone without reasonable suspicion or a warrant. The ruling was issued on September 17 in United States v. Alisigwe. As stated in a Bloomberg report, the decision does not concern Tunick or GrapheneOS directly. But it comes after the July case and adds to the debate around phone privacy, airport searches and electronic device searches at the US border.What happened at Atlanta airport in JanuarySamuel Tunick was returning from the Dominican Republic when federal agents stopped him at Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport on January 24, according to the case details you provided. The agents repeatedly asked him to unlock his phone and warned that it could be seized if he refused. After he entered a PIN, his phone reportedly went blank, flashed several times and appeared to restart. The data stored on the device was then lost.Prosecutors alleged that Tunick deliberately wiped the phone to prevent authorities from accessing potential evidence. His lawyers then argued that the underlying search was unlawful and sought to have the case dismissed. They also disputed the government's account of the incident.What does the new US court ruling say about phone searchesThe new ruling comes from the Second Circuit, which covers New York, Connecticut and Vermont. The case involved Chinwendu Alisigwe, a lawful permanent resident whose cellphone was searched by federal agents at John F. Kennedy International Airport in 2019 and again in 2021. Agents manually went through the phone and photographed information found on it.Alisigwe argued that the searches violated the Fourth Amendment because the government did not have a warrant. The appeals court rejected that argument.The court held that border agents do not need reasonable suspicion before manually searching a traveller's cellphone at the border. It said a cellphone is considered property for purposes of the existing border-search exception to the Fourth Amendment. The court also rejected the argument that the First Amendment creates a separate warrant requirement for cellphone searches at the border.Does this mean US border agents can search any phoneWhile the ruling is significant, its exact scope matters. The Second Circuit's decision concerns border searches of travellers' electronic devices. It does not mean police can generally search any person's phone anywhere in the US without legal restrictions.The court relied on the long-standing border-search exception, under which the government has broad authority to inspect people and property entering the country. The court said this authority extends to cellphones and that reasonable suspicion is not required for the type of manual cellphone search involved in the case.Judge Eunice Lee agreed with the result but wrote separately. She questioned the majority's broader conclusion that cellphone searches should be treated as routine searches requiring no suspicion, noting the amount of highly private information stored on modern phones.What about laptops and other electronic devicesThe ruling specifically concerned cellphone searches. The court's reasoning relies on the border-search exception and the treatment of a cellphone as property. So the headline question around phone and laptop searches needs some care: the decision does not specifically establish a separate rule for every type of electronic device in every situation.The broader legal issue is whether electronic devices carried across an international border receive special protection from warrantless searches. In this case, the Second Circuit said the Fourth Amendment does not require a warrant or reasonable suspicion for the cellphone search at issue.Why the July GrapheneOS case mattersThe Tunick case and the Alisigwe ruling involve different people, different airports and different legal proceedings. But both involve a growing question for travellers: what happens to the data on a phone when US authorities want to inspect it at the border?In Tunick's case, prosecutors allege that wiping the phone interfered with their ability to obtain evidence. In Alisigwe, the appeals court addressed the government's authority to search a cellphone in the first place. The two cases therefore highlight different sides of the same broader issue: government access to smartphones at international borders and the privacy protections available to travellers.Get the latest technology news and updates. articles.title: Huddersfield brass band exhibition hopes to inspire others
articles.summary: A brass band exhibition in Huddersfield is telling the story of 200 years of music and community.
articles.body:
"If I wasn't in a band, I'm not sure what I would have been doing. Twiddling my thumbs at home, probably," says Adrian Austin.

The University of Huddersfield music student began playing a brass instrument aged 12.

"I actually started playing the viola in primary school but when I went to high school they couldn't find me a strings teacher, so they gave me a euphonium instead.

Adrian's story is just one of many being told in a "world-first" exhibition at Heritage Quay in the town centre.

The exhibition 'That's Banding! 200 years of tradition and change', shows off items donated to the archive, believed to be the world's most extensive, over many decades, including concert programmes, photographs, trophies and hats.

A touchscreen plays memories of people involved in "banding" from across the country.

Austin's own experience is one of the more recent stories in a story stretching back about 200 years.

The young musician and conductor explains: "I think it's really important that people know about brass bands and come and watch us or give it a go themselves."

Sue Pope, from Brass Band England, wants other people to offer their experiences to the National Lottery-funded exhibition.

"You can bet your bottom dollar people have tons of stuff in their lofts and garages and don't know what to do with it," she says.

Pope explains that it is important to have a mix of voices to show brass bands are now more diverse - a particularly important point in her outreach work going into schools and music clubs.

"If we are encouraging people to take up a brass instrument its nice for people to see inspirational people who look like them and sound like them," she adds.

Kait Buchbaum is the archivist and exhibition curator.

She says that it is important to reflect a "vibrant, global culture that blends tradition with fresh creativity".

"Whilst bands and their members may change over time, the strong sense of community, contests, and shared heritage stays the same," she adds.

The exhibition will open on Saturday with exclusive tours of the archive and a Curator's Talk introducing the exhibition. It will remain at Heritage Quay until February.

articles.title: 'He's paying him back': Trump defends Russian oligarch funding his son's Bahamas wedding
articles.summary: US News: US President Donald Trump on Friday defended a Russian oligarch's role in funding celebrations around his son Donald Trump Jr's wedding in the Bahamas.
articles.body: US President Donald Trump on Friday defended a Russian oligarch's role in funding celebrations around his son Donald Trump Jr's wedding in the Bahamas, saying the arrangement was "totally allowed" but that his son had told him he was paying the money back.Trump said he had previously asked his son about Umar Kremlev, a Russian businessman with close ties to Russian president Vladimir Putin, after learning about his involvement in the wedding festivities."I asked about it. He said, 'No, I'm paying him back, Dad,'" Trump told reporters in the Oval Office. "So I heard he's paying him."Trump also said, "I hear he paid them back," without providing details on whether the repayment had already been completed.What Trump says about the wedding moneyProPublica reported earlier that Kremlev spent hundreds of thousands of dollars on expenses linked to the three-day Bahamas celebrations for Trump Jr and Bettina Anderson, including renting a private island and paying for a fireworks display. The report said the payments came through a Dubai-based entity affiliated with the International Boxing Association, which Kremlev heads.Trump defended the arrangement, saying it was common for friends to host wedding parties."It's totally allowed. And a lot of people have parties and all," he said, adding that he had himself given wedding parties for other people.Kremlev's involvement was subsequently confirmed by Bettina Trump in an Instagram post signed by the couple. She described him as a "dear friend" who had "very generously hosted two incredible nights of celebrations for us AFTER our wedding."She also stressed that she and Trump Jr. had married in a private ceremony surrounded only by family.Who is Umar Kremlev?Kremlev, who heads the International Boxing Association, has been publicly associated with Putin and Russia's political establishment. articles.body: Ellen DeGeneres and Portia de Rossi bought a 1917 farmhouse in Santa Barbara’s Toro Canyon in 2018 for $6.7 million, spent a year restoring its original character with modern touches, and sold it in 2019. The four bedroom, five bathroom home on about 25 acres has now returned to the market with a relisting price of $14.75 million, reflecting strong demand for private, land-rich estates in the Montecito and Carpinteria area. According to Homes of Celebs, the 4,313 square foot property blends historic farmhouse bones with the couple’s signature understated luxury, making it one of the most talked-about legacy listings in the region.A century-old farmhouse finds new lifeThe 1917 farmhouse sits in the quiet Toro Canyon corridor, a scenic stretch of rural Santa Barbara County known for avocado groves, vineyards and wide-open views toward the Pacific. When DeGeneres and de Rossi bought the property in 2018, the core structure already had more than a hundred years of history, but it needed careful updating to meet contemporary standards of comfort and design. Over the next year, the couple led a thoughtful restoration that preserved the home’s agricultural roots while introducing clean lines, natural materials and spaces suited to relaxed entertaining.Their approach focused on enhancing rather than erasing the past. Original beams, stone elements and rustic textures were kept in dialogue with new finishes such as wide-plank flooring, large-format windows and soft neutral palettes. The result was a residence that felt both grounded in its farming heritage and aligned with the couple’s signature style of understated luxury.From quick flip to long-term valueDeGeneres and de Rossi held the farmhouse for a relatively short period. After completing the renovation in 2019, they sold the property for about $6.98 million to Brian Robbins, the former CEO of Paramount Pictures and Nickelodeon. That transaction closed the couple’s direct involvement with the home, but it marked the beginning of the next chapter in the property’s story.Years later, the same farmhouse has returned to the market with a relisting price of $14.75 million. The increase reflects broader trends in the Santa Barbara luxury market, where buyers are willing to pay a premium for privacy, acreage and homes with authentic character. Properties in the Toro Canyon and Montecito areas have become especially sought after as high-profile purchasers look for estates that offer space, seclusion and a connection to the landscape.Inside the home todayCurrent listing details describe a residence of 4,313 square feet with four bedrooms and five bathrooms, arranged to maximise light and views across the 25-acre parcel. The layout balances formal and informal spaces, allowing for both quiet family living and larger gatherings. Outdoor areas extend the usable footprint, with terraces, gardens and room for animals or small-scale farming, echoing the property’s original purpose as a working farmhouse.Architectural highlights include high ceilings, generous room proportions and a flow that connects indoor and outdoor areas. The design language remains true to the couple’s initial vision, with natural materials, warm textures and a restrained colour scheme that lets the landscape take centre stage. For prospective buyers, the home offers a rare combination of history, renovation quality and a substantial landholding in one of California’s most tightly held luxury markets.Why this listing stands outThe farmhouse’s journey from a $6.7 million purchase to a $14.75 million relisting tells a larger story about the Santa Barbara real estate market. In less than a decade, well-located, character-rich properties with significant acreage have appreciated sharply, driven by limited supply and steady demand from entertainment, technology and business leaders. The DeGeneres and de Rossi name adds a layer of provenance, but the core appeal lies in the land, the architecture and the sense of retreat the estate provides.For buyers who value privacy over flash, the Toro Canyon location offers a quieter alternative to the more densely built sections of Montecito. The property’s size allows for multiple uses, from equestrian facilities to orchards or simply expansive lawns and walking paths. In a region where many estates sit on just a few acres, a 25-acre holding with a restored historic home is a uncommon find.A snapshot of a power couple’s property playbookThis farmhouse is one of many projects in DeGeneres and de Rossi’s wider real estate portfolio. Over the last two decades, the pair have bought, renovated and sold dozens of luxury homes across California, generating hundreds of millions in gains. Their strategy often involves identifying properties with strong bones or unique potential, investing in design-led upgrades and then moving on to the next opportunity.The Santa Barbara farmhouse fits that pattern. The couple acquired an older property, applied their design sensibility and market insight, and exited at a profit. Years later, the same home is testing the upper limits of what the local market will bear, offering a clear example of how heritage, location and brand can combine to drive value in Southern California’s most exclusive neighbourhoods.Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision? articles.title: EU urges US to lift travel ban on Palestinian delegation for UNGA meeting
articles.summary: The United Nations General Assembly will allow Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas to address via a prerecorded video.
articles.body:
The European Union says it regrets the denial of visas by the United States for the second year running to Palestinian Authority (PA) officials seeking to attend the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) in New York, urging it to reconsider the decision.

The statement on Saturday comes just days after the UNGA voted to allow Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas to address the body during the upcoming 81st session via a prerecorded statement.

“In light of its existing headquarters agreements with the UN and its obligations as host state, we urge the United States for this decision to be reconsidered,” said Anouar El Anouni, a spokesman for the EU’s diplomatic service.

On Friday, UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres also expressed regret at Washington’s decision, adding he was concerned about its impact “on the ability of the State of Palestine to participate fully in the work of the United Nations”.

The US Department of State announced on Wednesday that it would prolong visa sanctions on officials of the PA and members of the Palestine Liberation Organization (PLO).

“As a consequence of their failure to reform, contrary to their commitments to the United States, and their ongoing activities that undermine the prospects for peace, the United States will extend sanctions that deny visas to PLO members and PA officials,” the State Department said in a statement.

The department accused the PA of violating US law by bypassing direct negotiations to seek international recognition of Palestinian statehood.

It also cited the PA’s decision to take its dispute with Israel to international courts and its financial support for people the US and Israel label as convicted attackers and their families.

No Israeli officials face equivalent US travel restrictions, despite an International Criminal Court arrest warrant issued against Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu over alleged war crimes in Gaza.

Abbas’s address this year is expected to push for international recognition of Palestinian statehood and revive momentum for a two-state solution, building on a wave of formal recognitions by the United Kingdom, France, Canada and other Western nations last year.

His speech will also highlight the severe humanitarian crisis in Gaza alongside the rapid growth of illegal Israeli settlements and settler pogroms across the occupied West Bank.

Palestine’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Expatriates welcomed the UN resolution passed on Thursday allowing Abbas to address the assembly next week, saying it “represents a breaking of the attempt to prevent Palestine’s participation” in the UNGA’s annual session.

articles.title: Perth shark attack: Rare kill order issued as victim identified as Greg O'Neill
articles.summary: Greg O'Neill "loved the ocean", his family say, as police boats and helicopters patrol Perth's beaches in search of his body and the shark that attacked him.
articles.body:
A rare catch-and-kill order has been issued for a great white shark off the coast of Western Australia after 63-year-old swimmer Greg O'Neill was killed at a popular beach on Friday. His body has still not been found.

Authorities have said that beaches along the state's coast, including in the capital Perth, will remain closed until at least Sunday as the search for the shark continues.

It is the second shark attack in Western Australia (WA) this week, and the third fatal attack in the state this year.

The incident, at Sorrento Beach in Perth's north, has reignited debate about how to keep beachgoers safe in Australia.

In a statement, Greg O'Neill's family said they were "deeply shocked and devastated by the terrible tragedy."

"Greg loved the ocean and was known as a passionate swimmer, sports lover, dedicated worker and an all-round generous, witty guy."

On Saturday, his family visited the scene, where locals have been laying flowers.

Witness Jacqui Rapaic told the ABC that two men were swimming, but only one made it back to shore, and that she could see "a pool of blood" in the water.

Another witness told WAtoday that she saw the man being "mauled" as the shark "tossed him around like a fish". Members of the public reported seeing a 2.5m-long (8ft 2in) shark at around the same time.

Authorities in Perth's Joondalup area, where Sorrento is located, said all beaches were closed "as a precautionary measure" and would remain so until at least midday on Sunday.

Pictures on Saturday showed the coastline being patrolled by a police boat and helicopter.

Catch-and-kill orders are rare and controversial in Australia, where great white sharks are a protected species.

WA Fisheries Minister Jackie Jarvis said that she took the "extraordinary step" of issuing the order after the shark was spotted by water police on Saturday morning, and "positively identified as the shark involved in the incident".

The minister said she authorised fisheries officers to "destroy the shark" if it could be captured because of the "exceptional circumstances" of the attack and the "hazard posed by the shark".

It is believed to be the first time in 10 years that such an order had been issued in WA, Jarvis added, emphasising that the order was not a widespread cull as the state has seen in the past.

The minister also said that the use of drones and tagging would be increased to help protect beachgoers.

Catching and killing sharks has a long and controversial history in Western Australia - there were months of huge protests in 2014 when the state government authorised a cull after a spate of attacks.

The incident in Sorrento is the second in WA this week - on Monday a 56-year-old man was bitten while surfing off the coast of Geraldton, 430km (270 miles) north of Perth. He survived but lost part of his leg, another surfer who rescued him told the ABC.

There have been five fatal shark attacks in Australia this year.

A 12-year-old boy died after he was bitten in Sydney Harbour in January, and three divers were fatally mauled in separate incidents between May and June - two in Western Australia and the third in Queensland.

articles.title: Pakistan third from bottom in WEF gender gap index; women lag in workforce
articles.summary: Pakistan News: NEW DELHI: Pakistan has ranked 143rd among 145 economies in the World Economic Forum’s (WEF) Global Gender Gap Report 2026, placing it third from the .
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Pakistan has ranked 143rd among 145 economies in the World Economic Forum’s (WEF) Global Gender Gap Report 2026, placing it third from the bottom with 59.5% of its gender gap closed. Its score improved by 2.8 percentage points from 2025, marking the country's strongest year-on-year improvement in a decade, according to the report.The WEF index measures gender parity across four areas — economic participation and opportunity, educational attainment, health and survival, and political empowerment, media outlet Dawn cited.Pakistan's overall score has risen by 5.2 percentage points since 2006, when it stood at 54.3%. The WEF said the latest improvement was driven largely by gains in educational attainment.Women remain far behind men in workforceEconomic participation continued to be Pakistan's weakest area, with the country scoring 36.4% and ranking 144th globally. Labour-force participation stood at 34.6% parity, while women accounted for 6.5% of legislators, senior officials and managers and 44.9% of professional and technical workers.Parity in estimated earned income stood at 26.3%. The report also found that the share of women in senior leadership and business ownership remained limited.Education drives improvementPakistan recorded a significant improvement in educational attainment, reaching a parity score of 91.7%, more than six percentage points higher than in the previous edition.The WEF said parity in education has improved by 21 percentage points since 2006. Gains were recorded across primary, secondary and tertiary enrolment, making education the main driver of Pakistan's overall improvement in the 2026 index.Political representation remains lowPakistan scored 14.1% in political empowerment, ranking 107th globally. While parity in parliamentary and ministerial representation improved from the previous edition, women remained underrepresented in both areas.The report said women accounted for 21.69% of parliamentarians, while men made up 78.31%. Women held just 3.45% of ministerial positions, compared with 96.55% for men.Pakistan also received a score reflecting the period in which a woman has served as head of state, with the report noting that a female head of state had ruled the country for 4.73 of the previous 50 years.Legal rights show gapsThe report's contextual indicators also highlighted disparities in women's legal and economic rights. It found unequal rights relating to inheritance for widows and daughters and restricted rights in access to justice. Women were assessed as having near-equal rights regarding access to financial services and assets, while their rights relating to divorce and reproductive autonomy remained restricted.The report also recorded that 24.9% of women had experienced gender-based violence during their lives.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: US tightens H-1B scrutiny: Employers with layoffs face closer checks
articles.summary: US News: The Trump administration has ordered tighter scrutiny of H-1B visa applications where sponsoring employer companies have recently laid off, or plan to.
articles.body: The Trump administration has ordered tighter scrutiny of H-1B visa applications where sponsoring employer companies have recently laid off, or plan to lay off, similarly situated US workers. The move could bring greater scrutiny to companies that the administration alleges have cut American jobs while continuing to hire foreign workers.An executive order signed by President Donald Trump on September 18 directs the Departments of State, Labor and Homeland Security to consider whether a sponsoring employer “directly or indirectly” laid off employees within the previous year or plans future layoffs that “negatively affect the employment of similarly situated” American workers when adjudicating an H-1B labour condition application (LCA), petition, visa application or application for admission to the US.The proclamation states: “Many employers have laid off large numbers of highly skilled American workers, only to promptly hire large numbers of H-1B workers who are often lower-skilled and lower-paid. For instance, technology sector employers have collectively requested H-1B visas for hundreds of thousands of workers, yet have also laid off somewhere between 800,000 to 1.3 million American employees from 2022 through 2026. Employers have even forced laid off American workers to train their foreign replacements.”The White House said the H-1B programme was created to bring in specialised foreign workers to “supplement” the US economy, but alleged that it has instead been used by some employers to “undercut and displace” American workers. The accompanying proclamation similarly says the programme has been exploited to “replace, not supplement, American workers with lower-paid labour”. The executive order also calls for greater sharing of wage, employment, industry and other labour-market data among federal agencies when H-1B cases are assessed.“One company even warned its shareholders that restrictions on cheap H-1B labour could force the company to use ‘local’ workers, which may only be available at higher wages,” the executive order illustrates.An employer seeking to sponsor a foreign worker under the H-1B programme must first file a Labour Condition Application (LCA) with the US Department of Labor before submitting the H-1B petition to US Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS). In the LCA, the employer makes legally binding attestations covering matters including the wage to be paid, occupation, work location and working conditions.The executive order now directs the Department of Labor, within 30 days, to review data from previously filed LCAs to determine whether further action against sponsoring employers is warranted. The review could trigger investigations potentially bringing greater scrutiny to wages, job conditions and compliance with H-1B requirements.Mitch Wexler, senior counsel at Fragomen, a global immigration law firm, said: “It is not yet clear how the immigration agencies will implement these provisions. Existing law obligates high-volume H-1B employers (known as H-1B dependent) as well as those deemed to have wilfully violated H-1B programme rules to attest that they have not laid off a US worker and replaced them with an H-1B worker in an essentially equivalent job within 90 days before and after the filing of an H-1B petition or the placement of an H-1B worker with a secondary employer; under current law these requirements do not apply beyond this narrow class of H-1B employers.”“It is also not yet known how the agencies will consider economic data in the adjudication of H-1B filings, though this could result in higher scrutiny of offered wages, job duties, and job requirements, particularly in light of USCIS’ recent expansion of job requirement disclosures on the H-1B petition,” he added.The proclamation also takes aim at the outsourcing model, stating that many jobs held by H-1B workers eventually leave the US entirely. “Employers with outsourcing business models use teams of H-1B visa holders to replace US workers at third-party client businesses and liaise with other individuals working off-site from their country of origin. As soon as practicable, much of their own work is transferred offshore,” it states.The issue of layoffs and H-1B hiring has been the subject of earlier debate. In 2025, US senators Chuck Grassley and Dick Durbin questioned companies including TCS, Cognizant, Amazon, Microsoft, Google, Meta and Apple about their hiring and layoff practices. According to media reports, these companies disputed or rejected aspects of the assertions. The executive order moves the issue from a political debate to a course of action.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Buying a home in the US? How $0-down USDA mortgage works and who can qualify
articles.summary: Real Estate News: Buying a home in the US has become increasingly difficult as prices, mortgage costs and insurance expenses rise, but an often-overlooked government-ba.
articles.body: Buying a home in the US has become increasingly difficult as prices, mortgage costs and insurance expenses rise, but an often-overlooked government-backed loan allows eligible buyers to purchase a home with no down payment.The USDA-backed mortgage is available in areas that meet the programme's eligibility rules, and about 97% of US land mass falls within eligible areas, according to Ashley Harris, director of homebuyer education at Neighbors Bank, in an interview with New York Post. The figure does not mean 97% of Americans qualify, as borrowers must also meet income and other requirements.The programme is particularly notable because buyers do not necessarily have to live in what looks like a traditional rural area. Eligibility is largely determined by population density and specific geographic criteria.How the $0-down USDA mortgage worksThe USDA guaranteed loan allows eligible buyers to finance the entire purchase price of a home, eliminating the conventional down-payment requirement. Credit requirements can also be more flexible than those for some conventional mortgages.The programme dates back to the Great Depression, when the federal government sought to support rural communities and encourage home ownership outside major urban centres. Its reach has since expanded beyond traditionally rural areas.Under current rules, areas with populations below 10,000 generally qualify. Some communities with populations between 10,001 and 20,000 can also qualify if they are outside larger metropolitan areas and meet other conditions.Even some places with populations between 20,001 and 35,000 can be eligible if they previously had rural status, lost it because of population growth and still lack adequate affordable housing or mortgage credit.That means a property does not have to sit in an obviously rural setting to qualify. USDA boundaries can even cut through suburban areas, meaning homes on opposite sides of the same neighbourhood may have different eligibility.Who can qualify?The loan comes with income limits. For 2026, the standard limit is $122,800 for households of up to four people and $162,100 for households of five to eight people, although limits can be higher in expensive areas. Household income calculations generally include the income of all adult residents.The property must also be the borrower's primary residence. USDA loans cannot normally be used for vacation homes, second homes, investment properties or commercial properties.There are also conditions on the property itself. A standard USDA loan cannot be used to purchase a working farm, and homes must meet safety and structural requirements before approval. Buyers looking for a fixer-upper may therefore face additional hurdles.And "zero down" does not mean zero costs at closing. The programme carries a 1% upfront guarantee fee and a 0.35% annual fee based on the outstanding principal.For example, on a $350,000 home, the upfront fee would be $3,500, while the annual fee would initially be $1,225 and would be divided across monthly payments.Why the programme is attracting attentionThe option comes as affordability pressures continue to weigh on US homebuyers. About 43.5 million US households were considered cost-burdened in 2024, meaning they spent more than 30% of their income on housing, according to the Joint Center for Housing Studies at Harvard University.The median price of an existing single-family home reached about $434,800 in the second quarter of 2026, according to the National Association of Realtors.For buyers who struggle to accumulate a large down payment, the USDA programme can therefore remove one of the biggest upfront barriers to home ownership, provided the property, location and household meet the programme's rules.Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision? articles.title: Ole Miss, Lane Kiffin set for emotionally charged showdown 10 months after bitter split
articles.summary: Pete Golding will get a hero's welcome as Ole Miss hosts Lane Kiffin's LSU in a grudge match with fans flooding "The Grove" ahead of kickoff.
articles.body: A military flyover took place Friday afternoon over Oxford’s iconic Square ahead of Saturday’s matchup, when Ole Miss will welcome Lane Kiffin back to campus in a game 10 months in the making. Fans streamed through the area, buying up Ole Miss gear while making stops within local restaurants to kick their weekend off. There is nothing quite like Oxford, Mississippi, from its Southern charm to the small-town feel that defines it. An estimated 300,000 people are expected on campus today, with most of them partying in "The Grove" like it's going out of style. LANE KIFFIN'S RETURN TO OLE MISS COMES WITH BETRAYAL, LAWSUITS AND MEMORIES OF HIM TRYING TO BURN IT ALL DOWN ON WAY TO LSU The truth is, fans have had this weekend circled for 10 months. Ole Miss faithful are going to try to unleash nearly a year’s worth of aggravation over 24 hours, hoping to party into the early morning hours Sunday — or at least until local police kick them out around 1 a.m. CT — regardless of the outcome. Scenes that look more like something out of a John Grisham thriller tucked away in a small Mississippi town, it's not hard to notice how much this means to a fan base that has been put through the ringer over these past 10 months. 'HE'S DUST': OLE MISS STUDENTS RIP LANE KIFFIN AS LSU COACH PREPARES FOR HATRED IN OXFORD In reality, they have a team capable a competing for a national championship this season. But first, they have a lot to get off their chest when it comes to their former head coach, Lane Kiffin. Lane Kiffin knows he tarnished his reputation. But, he also embraces villain role A man who captivated a fan base, led them to heights rarely achieved and had them finally in the college football playoff after fumbling the opportunity in 2025, left them for a better job. But, it was how he left Ole Miss that will forever tarnish his legacy in Oxford. This, along with trying to take nearly every star on the Rebels football team, left fans with a worse feeling than had he just bolted for LSU without trying to burn it all down on the way out. Looking back, Lane has admitted to those around him that he should have handled the entire situation better. Maybe this weekend doesn’t contain as much vitriol. Maybe, Kiffin receives plenty of boos from the crowd, but deep down inside they are content with how things would have played out if he had chosen to act like a grown-up during the entire ordeal while contemplating whether to take the Florida or LSU job. But, we don't live in a "what if" world. We live in reality, and that will be welcomed by Lane on Saturday when he walks off the bus that is tucked away inside a fenced-in area just outside Vaught Hemingway Stadium. There is not much Ole Miss fans can say to Kiffin that he isn’t already prepared for. But, that doesn’t mean deep down inside it doesn’t bother him. As much as he loves playing the villain, he's still just a guy who feels lost at times without his father around any longer. THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW! Roaming around "The Grove" on Friday afternoon, Ole Miss fans had plenty to say about their former head coach, and the guy they worshiped for nearly six years. "Man, I'm not gonna lie bro, F--- Lane Kiffin," one Rebels fan said. "Lane Kiffin is 'K' bro. We smokin' him, no cap. Whatever Lane Kiffin did, it's bulls---. He could have waited to leave until after the season. Nah, he wanted to wait until he got us to the playoff to leave. "F--- Lane Kiffin, bro. And, f--- LSU." Saturday in Oxford will look like an action movie, with college football pageantry There's no denying we are about to witness one of the more cinematic scenes in this sport's history. I was in Austin last weekend as Arch Manning led Texas to the comeback win over Ohio State, and I'm still amazed at what I witnessed. But, even that monumental game does not have the built-in drama compared to what we will witness inside Vaught Hemingway Stadium. Lane Kiffin will stroll off the LSU bus later this afternoon, acting as if none of the noise is bothering him. He will walk into a stadium that he helped revitalize, alongside a number of assistant coaches on his LSU staff that helped him do it in this same town. On the other side, Pete Golding will receive a hero’s welcome when he takes his first steps onto the field in front of the Ole Miss student section. It's fitting. After the past ten months of buildup to this matchup that feels more like a heavyweight fight we used to witness in the late '90s. I'm fascinated to see how this plays out, alongside 60,000 fans wearing mostly powder blue and red, with a smattering of purple and gold. We made it. No more talking. No more jabs being traded through social media and television networks. articles.title: 2 Canada-based Gurdwaras sued over $13 million in loans linked to former Liberal MP Rajvinder Grewal
articles.summary: Rest of World News: Two Ontario gurdwaras are facing a lawsuit over more than $13 million in loans that were secured against their properties, adding another legal disput.
articles.body: Two Ontario gurdwaras are facing a lawsuit over more than $13 million in loans that were secured against their properties, adding another legal dispute to the growing list of cases involving lawyer and former Liberal MP Rajvinder Grewal.Sikh Spiritual Centre Toronto (SSCT) and Nanaksar Thath Ishar Darbar were sued in September by two companies seeking repayment of the loans. The case was filed in the Ontario Superior Court of Justice, Canadian media outlet The Globe and Mail reported.The dispute centres on loans arranged through RSG Law Professional Corporation, the law firm founded by Grewal. The companies allege that the firm failed to complete paperwork needed to properly secure part of the loans against the gurdwaras’ properties.The claims are part of a wider series of lawsuits involving Grewal and RSG Law. The combined value of the civil claims is more than $200 million, with some cases containing allegations of fraud. None of the allegations have been proven in court.According to court documents, SSMT Management Inc. provided a $10 million loan on April 25 last year secured against the property of Sikh Spiritual Centre Toronto. On May 20, the arrangement was increased to a $15 million commitment, with the additional amount to be secured against the Nanaksar property in Brampton.The loan carried an interest rate of up to 15% for the first six months, which amounted to about $187,500 a month. The rate was then set to increase to 24%, or about $300,000 a month.The lender alleges that Davinder Khattra, who operated RSG Law, was responsible for registering a second charge against the Brampton property but did not complete the process. The lender argues that this created uncertainty over whether the loan was properly secured.In a September 11 ruling, Ontario Superior Court Justice Frederick L. Myers ordered that the Brampton property could not be sold or used as security for another loan until a further hearing scheduled for January.There is also a dispute over whether the case has been resolved. Grewal’s lawyer, Simon Bieber, said in an emailed statement to The Globe and Mail that his understanding was that the matter had been resolved. Maria Naimark, the lawyer representing SSMT, said: “It has not been resolved.”Court records show that the gurdwaras also received money from RSG Law’s trust account in separate transactions.Records filed in proceedings before the Law Society of Ontario show that SSCT received $250,000 from RSG Law on April 7 and another $250,000 on April 10. A further $250,000 payment was made to Guru Nanak Darbar, another name for the Brampton gurdwara.In a separate case involving alleged cheque fraud against the Bank of Nova Scotia, another $250,000 transferred to SSCT was traced through RSG Law’s trust account.According to court filings, the money was part of more than $5.3 million transferred from lawyer Rajkiran Sidhu’s trust account after he received three cheques totalling $6.095 million. The bank later traced part of the money to RSG Law and, ultimately, to several recipients including SSCT.The bank has said in court documents that the $250,000 paid to SSCT has not been recovered.Both gurdwaras are federally registered charities. Public records also show that some members of their boards overlap, although it is unclear whether the disputed loans were intended to support charitable activities.Grewal is separately facing disciplinary proceedings before the Law Society of Ontario and has agreed not to practise law while the proceedings continue. Khattra and Sidhu are also facing disciplinary action.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Beloved restaurant chain dwindles from 850 locations to 87, but expert sees 'a lot of life left'
articles.summary: Friendly's once operated 850 restaurants, but 90% have closed. A Wharton marketing professor says nostalgia could fuel the ice cream chain's comeback.
articles.body: A casual-dining chain known for its ice-cream desserts, burgers and family atmosphere that once operated roughly 850 restaurants has dwindled to fewer than 100 locations in 11 states. Friendly's was founded as the "Friendly" ice-cream shop in Springfield, Massachusetts, by "spunky" brothers Prestley and Curtis Blake in 1935 — at the height of the Great Depression, according to the company's website. The two young entrepreneurs — Prestley was 20 years old and Curtis was just 18 — sold double-dip cones for 5 cents. FUDDRUCKERS BECAME THE 'BLOCKBUSTER' OF BURGERS, AND NOW IT'S NEARLY GONE In 1940, they expanded with a second location and began offering food, with hamburgers among the first additions to the menu. By 1951, there were 10 Friendly restaurants operating in Massachusetts and Connecticut, and by 1974, that number had grown to 500 restaurants across the Northeast and Mid-Atlantic. Friendly's marked its 90th year in business in 2025. Along the way, the company introduced new food and dessert items to its menu, began distributing its ice cream in supermarkets, set a Guinness World Record for the largest sundae in 1980 and added the apostrophe and "s" to its name in 1989. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS Friendly's also changed hands throughout the decades and filed for bankruptcy twice. Hershey's acquired Friendly's from the Blakes in 1979 and sold the chain nine years later to Tennessee Restaurant Company. By the mid-1990s, Friendly's had grown to about 850 restaurants. Friendly's first filed for bankruptcy in 2011 and again in November 2020. "Over the last two years, Friendly's has made important strides toward reinvigorating our beloved brand in the face of shifting demographics, increased competition and rising costs," then-Friendly's CEO George Michel said in a news release in 2020. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "Unfortunately, like many restaurant businesses, our progress was suddenly interrupted by the catastrophic impact of COVID, which caused a decline in revenue as dine-in operations ceased for months and re-opened with limited capacity." In 2021, Friendly's announced that Amici Partners Group, LLC had acquired the company and was "dedicated to reinvigorating 130-store restaurant chain." Today, 90% of Friendly's restaurants have closed, and there are 87 locations in 11 Eastern states, The Takeout reported. Twenty-two of the restaurants – or about 25% of them – are in Massachusetts. Some Friendly's restaurants were seen as old and tired and as failing to keep up with modern trends, Barbara E. Kahn, a marketing professor at the University of Pennsylvania's Wharton School, told Fox News Digital. Nevertheless, Kahn said there's "a lot of life left" in the Friendly's brand. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER "It has a legacy that could be built on and could serve to bring people in, especially on this trend of nostalgia, which can be a plus in restaurants," she said. "But it also has to keep up with changing times and changing tastes." Kahn said Friendly's has "positive DNA" the brand can build upon by capitalizing on the restaurants' nostalgia and strong brand legacy surrounding its ice cream, while also modernizing its offerings. "People who remember that brand from its heyday think of it as a fun place to go, a family restaurant known for its ice cream and fun food," she said. McDonald's is one brand Kahn pointed to as having stood the test of time by tweaking its offerings, adjusting to trends and maintaining fresh appeal. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ Kahn said adding more non-meat items, healthy grains and salads could possibly help Friendly's attract new customers. Fox News Digital reached out to Friendly's for comment.

articles.title: Mamata's 72-hour rollercoaster: Losing symbol, TMC name, candidate and then a breather on Day 3
articles.summary: India News: Once the dominant political force in West Bengal, Mamata Banerjee-led Trinamool Congress has found itself navigating an unusually turbulent stretch, w.
articles.body: Once the dominant political force in West Bengal, Mamata Banerjee-led Trinamool Congress has found itself navigating an unusually turbulent stretch, with the party facing questions over its identity, leadership and ability to hold its organisation together.For Mamata Banerjee, almost synonymous with the Trinamool Congress after years of being its most powerful face, the past 72 hours have been particularly bruising.First came the Election Commission's decision over the party's name and symbol. Then came a candidate's withdrawal in Nandigram. A second candidate in Rejinagar announced his exit, only to reverse the decision within hours.By Saturday, at least one crisis had been defused. But the sequence of events has underlined how quickly the political landscape around Mamata's party has changed.From 'grass and flowers' to 'footballer'The biggest blow came when the Election Commission allotted the 'footballer' symbol to Mamata's faction of the Trinamool Congress and assigned it the name 'Mamata All India Trinamool Congress'.The move came amid a bitter dispute over the party's identity and its traditional 'flowers-and-grass' symbol.The rival faction led by once-a-Didi-loyalist Arup Roy was allotted the name 'Democratic Trinamool Congress' and the 'envelope' symbol.For a party that has built much of its political identity around Mamata and the familiar twin-flower-and-grass symbol, the change was more than a technical electoral decision. It forced the party to enter an election with a new name and a symbol that voters would have to recognise.The developments followed Mamata's unsettling defeat at the hands of the BJP in the assembly polls, after which the party was left vulnerable to rebellion and splits in both the state assembly and Parliament.The internal churn went a step further when the rebel faction sought to stake its claim over the Trinamool Congress identity, after the party had ruled Bengal for 15 straight years.Nandigram delivers another shockThe trouble then moved from the party's identity to its candidates.Mamata's choice for the Nandigram bypoll, Sanchita Pradhan Dey, withdrew her candidature after meeting chief minister Suvendu Adhikari.Dey, who had lost her job in connection with the teacher recruitment scam, met Adhikari along with her husband Satyajit before withdrawing her nomination a day ahead of the deadline.The reasons for her decision were not immediately clear.For Mamata's camp, however, the timing could hardly have been comfortable. The party was already dealing with the fallout from the Election Commission's decision and internal rebellion when its candidate in a politically significant constituency stepped away from the contest.Faced with a sudden vacancy, Mamata announced support for Congress's Nandigram candidate Milan Pradhan, describing the Congress as a "sister party".The move was projected as an attempt to strengthen the INDIA bloc ahead of the October 6 bypolls.But that plan too ran into trouble.Hours later, Pradhan was arrested in connection with criminal cases lodged against him during the 2007 anti-land acquisition movement in Nandigram in Purba Medinipur district.Didi and her camp accused the BJP government of "acting in an authoritarian manner to crush dissent and win the bypoll by a huge margin".BJP leader and Union minister Sukanta Majumdar hit back, saying such allegations were expected from a "party centred on one person, whose activists had carried out attacks on the then opposition BJP after the 2021 assembly polls".Nandigram seat has also been a bastion of CM Suvendu Adhikari.Rejinagar's dramatic U-turnIf Nandigram was not enough, Rejinagar added another twist.Rabiul Alam Chowdhury, a former TMC MLA and the party's candidate for the Rejinagar bypoll, announced on Saturday that he was withdrawing from the contest.His explanation offered a glimpse into the difficulties facing the party's grassroots organisation."It is becoming difficult for me to motivate grassroots workers who have been facing regular harassment. Police have arrested many of our workers, slapping false cases. Also, it is an onerous task to familiarise the electorate with the new 'footballer' symbol in such a short time. In this given situation, I informed Mamata di last evening about my decision (not to contest)... Let's see," he said.For a brief period, it appeared that Mamata had lost another candidate.Then, about an hour and a half later, Chowdhury called another presser and reversed his decision.He said the party's top leadership, including Mamata herself, had spoken to him and persuaded him to stay in the contest."I will be contesting the bypoll. We are in Didi's party and we cannot do anything outside her wishes. So, following Didi's instructions, I am retaining my candidature," Chowdhury said.He said Mamata had directed him not to withdraw.The sudden reversal brought a temporary pause to what had been a relentless sequence of setbacks.'Footballer' symbol, old party machineryChowdhury subsequently visited the Beldanga police station and met officers.Emerging from the police station, he said the police administration had assured him and party workers of security during the campaign."I have been assured of security by the police after the supremo (Mamata) intervened. I have met officers of the Beldanga police station and they have also assured me and my cadre of security during campaigning," he said.Chowdhury also sought to reassure his supporters that the campaign would go ahead despite the turbulence."Even if only 10 workers stand by me, I will take them along and begin a door-to-door campaign," he said, adding that he expected all necessary assistance in accordance with Mamata's instructions.His return to the contest gave Mamata's camp at least one piece of good news after three days of political turbulence.The troubling sequence unfolded over 72 hours, turning into an unsettling rollercoaster for Didi.The bypolls for Bengal seats is scheduled for October 6.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: A 6-year-old Michigan girl followed the family dogs into the woods and vanished for 4.5 hours; a relative's trail camera spotted her half a mile away, and rescuers found her safe beside one dog
articles.summary: US News: A 6-year-old girl in Michigan’s Upper Peninsula disappeared for four and a half hours after following her family dogs into the woods, sparking a large.
articles.body: A 6-year-old girl in Michigan’s Upper Peninsula disappeared for four and a half hours after following her family dogs into the woods, sparking a large overnight search that involved police, fire crews, K-9 units and drones. The breakthrough came when a relative’s trail camera, set up about half a mile from the home, captured an image of the child moving through the trees. Rescuers then located her safe and calm, sitting beside one of the dogs near Ski Hill Road in Forsyth Township, according to reports from EUP News and The Daily Press.A quiet evening turns urgentThe incident unfolded on a Wednesday evening near County Road 456 in Little Lake, Marquette County. Payton Kagarise had just finished dinner and helped bake a cake when she asked to let the family dogs out. Her great-grandmother, Diana, said she told Payton not to let the dogs loose because they were not used to the road, and her husband went up the back hill to call her back. By the time he reached the top, Payton was gone.The family searched the property and nearby roads, calling for Payton and the dogs, but found nothing. Within about ten minutes of realising she was missing, they called 911. Dispatchers sent emergency units to the intersection of County Road 456 and Setter Drive at around 8:25 p.m., and a coordinated search began under the cover of night.A multi-agency search in the darkForsyth Township Police, Fire and EMS joined forces with the Marquette County Sheriff’s Office Special Operations Division, which deployed K-9 teams, search and rescue personnel and thermal drones. Michigan State Police added resources from the Negaunee and Gladstone posts, including specialised K-9 and drone operators from the Tactical Support Team, as well as an aviation unit to scan the area from the air. Community members and family also joined the effort, combing through dense woods and along rural roads.Hours passed as crews worked methodically through the forested terrain. The search area was challenging, with thick vegetation and uneven ground that can be difficult to navigate even in daylight. As the operation stretched into the late evening and then past midnight, the focus remained on covering as much ground as possible while following any potential trail that might point to Payton’s direction of travel.The trail camera clueThe turning point came when a family member received a cellular alert from a private trail camera located roughly half a mile south of where Payton had vanished. The camera had captured an image confirming that the 6-year-old had moved through that part of the woods. That single frame gave incident commanders a much clearer idea of where to concentrate their resources.Search assets were immediately redirected toward the area near Ski Hill Road. With the new information in hand, crews were able to narrow their grid and move more quickly through the most promising sections of forest. Within a short time after shifting the search, they closed in on Payton’s location.Found safe beside a dogWhen rescuers reached Payton, they found her sitting in the woods beside one of the family dogs. The second dog was recovered shortly afterward. According to Trooper Aaron Griffin of the Michigan State Police, one of the first responders on the scene, Payton was calm and unafraid. He asked her if she was scared, and she simply said no. Her family described her as a brave little girl who had followed the dogs because she did not want them to get lost.Payton’s mother, Tiana Sicotte, said her daughter told them the dog started running off and she followed. The reunion was emotional, according to EUP News. Tiana said she cried and held her daughter tightly, overwhelmed with relief. Her husband, Tim Sicotte, described the moment of being brought back together as a return to safety, back in mom and dad’s arms after hours of fear and uncertainty.Why the story resonatesCases like this highlight how quickly a routine evening can turn into a crisis when a young child wanders into rural or wooded areas. Payton’s decision to follow the dogs is understandable from a child’s perspective. She saw her pets moving away and wanted to keep them safe, not realising how far she was going or how hard it would be for adults to find her in the dark.The successful outcome also underscores the value of coordinated emergency response and community involvement. Multiple agencies worked together through the night, using ground teams, dogs, drones and aircraft. The trail camera, a piece of technology many rural residents use to monitor wildlife or property, became a critical tool in narrowing the search and bringing Payton home.Lessons for families and neighboursForsyth Township Police and Emergency Services thanked all the agencies, community members and family who took part in the search. Their statement emphasised how the combined effort, along with a bit of luck from the trail camera alert, helped bring the child back safely. For other families in rural or semi-rural areas, the incident is a reminder to set clear boundaries for young children around pets and wooded areas, and to ensure that properties have ways to quickly alert neighbours and emergency services if a child goes missing.Payton’s story ends with relief rather than tragedy. She was found in good health, reunited with her parents and able to go back to the normal rhythm of school, family and life in the Upper Peninsula. For the rescuers who spent hours in the cold night woods, the sight of a calm 6-year-old sitting beside a dog was the best possible outcome after a long and anxious search.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: After deaths of nine women, South Africans gather to run, mourn and demand change
articles.summary: South Africans gathered for memorial runs and protests this week after ​the killings of nine women near Johannesburg reignited anger and fear over violence that many ‌say mirrors the dangers women face every day.
articles.body: South Africans gathered for memorial runs and protests this week after ​the killings of nine women near Johannesburg reignited anger and fear over violence that many ‌say mirrors the dangers women face every day. Police have found the bodies of nine women in Ekurhuleni, east of Johannesburg, over the past two months and are investigating whether the killings are linked. Most of the victims were in their 20s and ​30s. Some were found stripped of their clothes and showed signs of sexual assault. A memorial run ​in Johannesburg on Saturday morning honoured one of the victims, Elizabeth Moselakgomo, who ⁠disappeared after going for a run and was found dead days later. Runners lit candles and carried ​a banner reading: “Enough. Stop Femicide.” “We are here because we’ve lost a runner. But we are not safe anywhere,” ​said Lerato Lentsela, one of dozens of people who dressed in black for the memorial run. “We are not safe running, we are not safe at a post office, we are not safe on a date, we are not safe in ​our own homes, we are not safe in an Uber.” The killings have reignited anger over violence against ​women in South Africa, where gender-based violence was declared a national disaster in 2025. Many women say the heightened attention and ‌official ⁠promises have done little to make them feel safer. “Enough is enough. Our women deserve to live, walk, run and exist without fear,” the Uyinene Mrwetyana Foundation, a charity that campaigns against gender-based violence, said in a statement. President Cyril Ramaphosa said on Thursday that South Africa could not allow itself to grow accustomed to ​such violence and pledged that ​no stone would be ⁠left unturned in the investigations. But policing in South Africa is weakened by corruption and lack of resources. Only about one in 10 murders is ever solved. “We need ​to relook at our policing. The only reason these nine women were found ​was because ⁠there was more police presence in the area. This problem is countrywide,” said Merlize Jogiat of Women for Change, which held a memorial event in Cape Town on Friday. Some women also criticised police advice urging them to ⁠take extra ​precautions when exercising or walking alone. “Stop placing the responsibility of ​our safety back onto us,” Women for Change said in a social media post. “Women should not have to organise their entire lives ​around surviving violence and not being next.”
